p2A:
The Last Light on Gull Island

Every evening for forty-one years, Elias Morrow climbed the one hundred and twelve steps of the Gull Island lighthouse and lit the lamp. He did it in summer, when the sea lay flat and silver like a sheet of tin, and he did it in winter, when the wind threw salt against the glass so hard that it sounded like gravel. He never missed a night. Not once.

His granddaughter, Nora, came to live with him the spring she turned twelve. Her mother had taken a job in the city, the kind of job that kept her on trains and in hotels, and so Nora arrived on the supply boat with a single suitcase, a box of books, and a look on her face that said she had already decided to hate everything.

"There's no internet," she said on the first night, holding her phone up toward the ceiling as if the signal might be hiding in the rafters.

"There's the sea," Elias said. "It's older than the internet, and it has better stories."

Nora rolled her eyes so hard that Elias was afraid they might stay that way.

For the first few weeks she barely spoke. She read on the rocks below the lighthouse, wrapped in two sweaters, and she ate her dinner without looking up. But every evening, at exactly the same time, she heard her grandfather's slow steps on the iron staircase, and every evening she noticed the beam sweep across the water, white and steady, reaching out toward ships she could not see.
p2B:
One night in May, curiosity won. She followed him up.

The lamp room was smaller than she had imagined, and warmer. The great lens sat in the middle like a giant glass beehive, its rings catching the last of the sunset and breaking it into a hundred tiny rainbows. Elias wiped each panel with a soft cloth, checked the oil, wound the old clockwork that turned the light, and finally struck a long match.

"Why do you still do it by hand?" Nora asked. "Couldn't a machine do all this?"

"A machine could," he said. "And one day a machine will. The government has already sent the letters." He nodded toward a drawer stuffed with envelopes. "Next autumn they'll put in an automatic lamp, and I'll be sent to live on the mainland like a retired horse."

"Does that make you sad?"

Elias watched the beam reach the horizon and come back. "A light doesn't care who lights it," he said at last. "But the people who need it should know that someone is awake. That's the part a machine can't do."
p3:
After that night, Nora climbed the stairs with him every evening. He taught her how to trim a wick, how to read the barometer, how to tell a fishing boat from a cargo ship by the pattern of its lights. He taught her the names of the stars that sailors steered by, and the names of the ships that had sunk on the reef before the lighthouse was built. She wrote everything down in a notebook with a green cover, and slowly the notebook filled.

She also began to notice things on her own. The way the gulls went quiet an hour before a storm. The way the fog crept in from the east like a cat that did not want to be seen. The way her grandfather rubbed his left hand when the weather turned cold, and pretended he wasn't.

In October, the storm came.

It arrived faster than the radio had promised, a black wall moving across the water. By late afternoon the waves were breaking over the lower rocks, and the whole tower hummed with the wind. Elias started up the stairs at the usual time, but halfway up he stopped, gripped the rail, and sat down heavily on a step.
p4A:
"Grandpa?"

"It's nothing," he said, but his face was grey and his breath came short. "Just my heart reminding me how old it is. Give me a minute."

Nora looked up the spiral of the staircase, then out of the narrow window. Through the rain she could see a small light on the water, rising and falling. A boat. Too close to the reef.

"I'll do it," she said.

"Nora, the wind up there—"

"I know how. You taught me."

She climbed the last fifty steps two at a time. In the lamp room the glass shook in its frame, and the noise was so loud that she could not hear her own breathing. Her hands trembled as she checked the oil and wound the clockwork, exactly the way she had watched him do it a hundred times. The first match blew out. So did the second. She cupped the third against her chest, counted to three, and touched it to the wick.

The flame caught. The lens woke up. And the beam swung out across the black water, white and steady, as if nothing in the world could stop it.

She stood at the window and watched the small boat. For a long, terrible moment it kept heading straight for the reef. Then, slowly, it turned. It found the channel. It slipped past the rocks and disappeared into the safety of the harbour.
p4B:
When she came down, her grandfather was still sitting on the step. He did not ask whether she had done it. He had seen the light on the wall.

"Someone was awake," he said quietly, and squeezed her hand.

The next morning the fisherman from the boat rowed out to the island with a basket of fresh bread and a jar of honey. He said he had lost his engine and his radio, and that he had been sure he would die. "Then the light came on," he said, "and I knew which way was home."

The automatic lamp was installed the following spring, just as the letters had promised. Elias moved to a small house in the harbour town, where he could see the lighthouse from his kitchen window. Nora moved there too. Her mother came home more often now, and sometimes all three of them sat on the sea wall in the evening to watch the beam come on by itself.

It was never quite the same. But every night, at exactly the time her grandfather used to climb the stairs, Nora looked out toward Gull Island and said, very softly, "I'm awake."

And somewhere out on the dark water, she liked to think, someone was glad.
